s: The Peloponnesians pursued Conon's fleet and fought the Athenians near Mitylene. They forced many Athenians ashore, later overcame the Athenian position in the harbour, and helped Callicratides besiege the city.

s: Mitylene contained an Athenian garrison and was reached by Conon after the naval engagement. The city received Athenians and Mityleneans from the countryside, prepared for defense, and was then surrounded by Callicratides.

s: After gaining control of the harbour outside the walls, Callicratides landed his men and besieged Mitylene on every side. The city had prepared defenses and was strengthened by Athenians and Mityleneans who entered it for protection.

l: naval battle at Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Conon initially attacked part of Callicratides' larger fleet near Mitylene after drawing its leading ships away from the rest. Callicratides eventually brought the whole fleet together, forced Conon into the inner harbour, and gained control of the harbour outside the city walls.

l: Hermocrates' attempted return to Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Hermocrates returned from Selinus with three thousand armed men after being summoned by members of his faction. His plan was discovered, the Syracusans assembled in arms, and Hermocrates and many accomplices were killed; the surviving participants were condemned to banishment.

s: The Lacedaemonian fleet delivered to Callicratides numbered 150 ships after additions from other places, while Conon's Athenian fleet numbered seventy ships. The fleets fought near Mitylene, and Callicratides ultimately captured thirty ships and secured the harbour.

l: harbour at Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Conon blocked the harbour entrance with stone-filled vessels and ships fixed by anchors, while defending the shallows and the open passage. Callicratides eventually drove the Athenians from their position, entered the harbour, and anchored close to Mitylene.

s: The Carthaginians prepared a large invasion of Sicily after earlier successes, building Therma and assembling troops, warships, and transport vessels under Hannibal and Amilcar. A Syracusan naval force defeated part of the Carthaginian fleet at Eryx, but Hannibal then sailed toward Sicily to protect the army’s transport. The Syracusans sought aid from the Greeks in Italy and the Lacedaemonians, while the Agrigentines gathered their food and valuables inside Agrigentum. The unit describes Agrigentum’s wealth, temples, public works, lavish customs, and prominent citizens, especially Gellias, before noting the city’s vulnerability and the luxury of its inhabitants during the siege.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Sicily was the intended target of the Carthaginians, who aimed to subdue all its cities. The island’s cities were alarmed by the scale of the Carthaginian preparations.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Carthage received Syracusan ambassadors seeking peace but gave a doubtful answer. It later assembled a major army, equipped warships, and gathered about a thousand transport ships for operations in Sicily.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The Carthaginians built Therma near the hot springs in Sicily after gathering people from Carthage and other African cities who were willing to transplant themselves. They recruited soldiers from Spain, the Balearic islands, Libya, Africa, allied nations, and Italy, and prepared to conquer the Sicilian cities.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The Syracusans sent ambassadors to Carthage to complain about the previous war and seek peace. Their fleet fought the Carthaginians at Eryx, sinking fifteen Carthaginian ships, and they sought military assistance from the Greeks in Italy and the Lacedaemonians.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Hannibal, who had previously razed Selinus and Himera, was appointed general of the Carthaginian forces with full authority over the war. After the naval defeat at Eryx, he sailed with fifty galleys to make the Syracusan victory fruitless and help secure the transport of the army.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Because Hannibal pleaded old age, Amilcar, son of Hanno and a member of the same family, was joined with him in command. Amilcar and Hannibal consulted together and arranged the recruitment of soldiers from several regions.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Agrigentum was a wealthy city whose inhabitants expected to bear the first pressure of the Carthaginian war. Its people brought grain, other produce, and valuables from the surrounding country into the city, which was later described as having magnificent temples, a large artificial pond, grand tombs, and a large population.

l: Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The Agrigentines were prosperous through vineyards, olive production, and trade with the Libyans, and they displayed their wealth in buildings, entertainments, clothing, and precious household objects. During the siege they were so accustomed to luxury that a decree limiting guards to a bed, tent, woollen mantle, and two pillows was considered harsh.

l: Agrigentum campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The campaign threatened Agrigentum first because of the city’s position and wealth. The Agrigentines prepared for the danger by moving food and valuables inside the city, while the Carthaginian preparations caused widespread fear.

l: Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The Carthaginians prepared an invasion of Sicily by raising a very large army and assembling warships and transport vessels. Their first fleet action near Eryx ended with fifteen Carthaginian ships sunk, but Hannibal sailed afterward to support the planned crossing.

l: Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The Carthaginian army was recruited from Carthaginians, Africans, Spaniards, Balearic islanders, allied Mauretanians and Numidians, people near Cyrene, and Campanians hired from Italy. Timaeus estimated it at somewhat more than 120,000 men, while Ephorus gave a figure of 300,000.

l: Gellias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Gellias was described as the richest of the Agrigentines at that time. He built rooms for public entertainment, invited passing strangers into his house, once clothed and entertained five hundred Gelonian horsemen, and possessed an enormous wine cellar and cistern; despite his wealth, he had a mean appearance and was known for ingenuity.

l: temple of Jupiter Olympus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The temple of Jupiter Olympus at Agrigentum was near completion when the war stopped its construction, and it was never finished after the city was sacked. It was described as 340 feet long, 60 feet wide, and 120 feet high above its foundation, with walls and large exterior and interior pillars, and carvings depicting the giants’ war and the destruction of Troy.

l: Agrigentum's temples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: The temples of Agrigentum, especially the temple of Jupiter, testified to the grandeur and wealth of the city’s people. Most of the other sacred buildings had been burned or destroyed by repeated storming of the city.

l: Agrigentines' wealth and luxury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XII.
s: Agrigentines’ wealth came partly from vineyards, olive groves, and the sale of olives to Carthage, and it was displayed in temples, tombs, chariots, gold clothing, and gold and silver vessels. Their luxurious habits extended to public feasts, weddings, hospitality, and military life, where even basic restrictions on guards’ sleeping arrangements were resented.

s: The Carthaginians besieged Agrigentum in Sicily after the Agrigentines rejected offers of alliance or neutrality. Under Amilcar and Hannibal, they attacked the city, but Syracusan forces under Daphnaeus defeated the Carthaginian army at the Battle of the Himera and relieved the siege temporarily. A Carthaginian naval attack then destroyed the Syracusan grain fleet, after which the besieged Agrigentines suffered famine, evacuated, and abandoned many of their sick and elderly. Amilcar entered and sacked Agrigentum, killing many inhabitants and carrying its immense wealth and artworks to Carthage.

s: The Carthaginians landed their forces in Sicily, marched against Agrigentum, and divided their army between a hill camp and a fortified camp near the city. After their offers of alliance or neutrality were rejected, they besieged the city, later overcame its defenses through famine, and plundered Agrigentum.

l: Agrigentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The Agrigentines rejected the Carthaginians' proposed alliance and neutrality, mobilized their able-bodied population, and defended their city. After prolonged resistance and the loss of outside support, they suffered severe famine, evacuated toward Gela, and were later given Leontium by the Syracusans for habitation.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Agrigentum was besieged by the Carthaginians and defended by its inhabitants, assisted by Dexippus, Syracusan forces, and other allies. Its population eventually evacuated because of famine, after which Amilcar entered, killed many who remained, and stripped the city of its wealth, religious treasures, pictures, and statues.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Sicily was the place where the Carthaginians landed their army and began their campaign against Agrigentum.

l: Amilcar the Carthaginian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Amilcar commanded the Carthaginians with Hannibal during the siege of Agrigentum. He ordered assaults and the construction of siege works, sacrificed to the gods when plague struck his army, defeated the Syracusan grain fleet through a naval ambush, and entered and plundered Agrigentum after its evacuation.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Hannibal commanded the Carthaginian siege with Amilcar and ordered the destruction of monuments and tombs to build mounds against the walls. He died during the plague that broke out in the Carthaginian army.

l: Dexippus the Lacedaemonian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Dexippus, a Lacedaemonian living at Gela, came to the aid of the Agrigentines with five hundred soldiers and directed their defense. He later joined the council of war, was accused of treachery, and was reported to have accepted fifteen talents to advise the Italian commanders to withdraw from Agrigentum.

l: Daphnaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Daphnaeus was appointed general of the Syracusan relief army, which included forces from Italy, Messana, Camarina, Gela, and elsewhere. He defeated the Carthaginian army after it crossed the Himera and then encamped in the enemy's former position, but restrained his troops from pursuing too far.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The Syracusans sent an army and fleet to aid the besieged Agrigentines, fearing a fate like that of Himera and Selinus. Their army defeated the Carthaginians at the Himera, but their grain fleet was subsequently attacked and captured by Amilcar; they later gave Leontium to the displaced Agrigentines.

l: Campanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The Campanians hired by the Agrigentines had previously served under Amilcar and guarded the hill Athenea. During the famine they demanded bread from Amilcar, and after the Syracusan grain fleet was defeated, they accepted fifteen talents and defected to the Carthaginians.

l: Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Gela was where Dexippus lived in high esteem and from which he brought five hundred soldiers to aid Agrigentum. The Agrigentines who evacuated their city were escorted to Gela, and its roads and surrounding country filled with the refugees.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Carthage received the choicest spoils taken from Agrigentum, including the Phalarian bull. The text later says that Scipio Africanus found the bull at Carthage when the city was destroyed and restored it to the Agrigentines.

l: Agrigentum campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The siege began after the Agrigentines rejected Carthaginian proposals for alliance or neutrality. The Carthaginians used towers, siege mounds, and attacks, while the Agrigentines received aid from Syracusans and other allies; after the Syracusan grain fleet was destroyed and famine spread, the defenders withdrew.

l: Battle of the Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: At the Battle of the Himera, Daphnaeus led the Syracusan army against the Carthaginians and their allies. The Syracusans won after a long engagement, killed more than six thousand of the opposing soldiers, and pursued the survivors to their camp.

l: Carthaginian naval attack on the Syracusan grain fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Amilcar sent forty galleys from Panormus and Motya to ambush the Syracusan ships carrying grain to Agrigentum. The Carthaginians sank eight ships and drove the rest ashore, capturing the fleet and transforming the situation in their favor.

l: Agrigentum's fall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: Agrigentum fell after its defenders and inhabitants were weakened by famine and the departure of their allied forces. Amilcar entered the abandoned city, killed almost everyone he found, and destroyed or removed its religious and civic wealth.

l: evacuation of Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The Agrigentines decided to leave after discovering that the city lacked sufficient provisions. Many men, women, and children reached Gela under military guard, while the sick, elderly, and others unable to leave were abandoned; some inhabitants killed themselves rather than depart.

l: the sack of Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: During the sack of Agrigentum, Amilcar's forces killed inhabitants who remained, including people who sought refuge in temples. They plundered religious and secular places, seized paintings, statues, immense wealth, and the Phalarian bull, sending the finest spoils to Carthage.

l: Syracusan grain fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, As wc were not willing to let these things pass altogether, so we shall
s: The Syracusan grain fleet carried abundant corn intended for Agrigentum. It was attacked unexpectedly by Amilcar's forty galleys in winter; eight ships were sunk and the remainder were driven ashore and captured.
