s: After Agrigentum fell to the Carthaginians, panic spread through Sicily and Syracuse. Dionysius, the son of Hermocrates, accused Syracuse's commanders of treachery, gained command, secured the recall of the exiles, and used the crisis to increase his influence. He obtained sole command, raised a personal guard and mercenary force, and eventually declared himself king of Syracuse. The Syracusans feared tyranny but were unable to resist him while the Carthaginians threatened the city.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: Syracuse received refugees from Sicily after the fall of Agrigentum and became the center of resistance to the Carthaginians. Dionysius used the city's fear and political divisions to obtain absolute authority over it.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: The Syracusans blamed the Sicilians and their commanders for the disasters surrounding Agrigentum, then removed their commanders and chose Dionysius among their replacements. They later granted Dionysius sole and absolute command, recognized the danger of tyranny, and were unable to oppose him when he declared himself king.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: Agrigentum was captured after an eight-month siege shortly before the winter solstice. The Carthaginians plundered it, burned its temples, removed its valuable dedicated objects, and occupied it through the winter.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: The Carthaginians captured and destroyed Agrigentum and then prepared engines and weapons for further campaigns. They planned to attack Gela first in the following spring and maintained a large army near Syracuse.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: The fall of Agrigentum spread terror throughout Sicily. Some Sicilians fled to Syracuse, while others moved with their families and possessions to Italy.

l: exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: Dionysius persuaded the Syracusans to recall the exiles so they could help defend their country. He regarded them as politically changeable and useful to his ambition, and they returned after the decree was published.

l: Agrigentum's fall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: Agrigentum's fall caused widespread panic and led refugees to seek safety in Syracuse or Italy. It also intensified accusations against Syracuse's commanders and enabled Dionysius to present himself as a necessary defender.

l: the war against Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: The war against Carthage produced fear, political accusations, and repeated preparations at Syracuse. Dionysius used the danger posed by the Carthaginians to justify recalling exiles, increasing soldiers' pay, and receiving sole command.

l: Dionysius's seizure of power, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: Dionysius's seizure of power proceeded through accusations against rival commanders, control of soldiers, the creation of a personal guard, and the recruitment of mercenaries and exiles. He removed or sent away potential opponents and openly declared himself king after securing Syracuse with armed forces.

l: tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 3(111.
s: The Syracusans recognized that granting Dionysius sole command would lead to tyranny, although they had helped create the situation. Dionysius then used his guard, mercenaries, political alliances, and control of the city to establish himself as ruler.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenians defeated the Lacedaemonians in the great naval battle of Arginusae, though a storm prevented the recovery and burial of many dead. Callicratides was killed while fighting bravely, and the Peloponnesian fleet was routed. The Athenians later condemned eleven commanders to death for failing to bury the dead, including Diomedon, despite their victory. Sophocles died at about ninety years of age, after winning eighteen dramatic victories.

l: battle of Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The battle was fought between an Athenian fleet of 150 ships and a Lacedaemonian fleet of 140 ships near the islands of Arginusae. The Athenians won, losing twenty-five ships, while the Peloponnesians lost seventy-seven.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenians admitted strangers and foreigners to their city, raised a fleet of 150 ships, and defeated the Lacedaemonians at Arginusae. They later condemned their commanders for failing to bury the dead, although the failure resulted from a violent storm.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Lacedaemonians sent a fleet of 140 well-manned ships under Callicratides to relieve the siege of Mitylene. Their fleet was defeated at Arginusae after Callicratides was killed, and the survivors fled toward Chios and Cuma.

l: Callicratides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Callicratides commanded the Lacedaemonian fleet and accepted the reported prophecy that he would die, declaring that his death would not obscure the glory of Sparta. He fought fiercely, disabled or sank several enemy ships, and was killed after his vessel became fastened to Pericles the younger’s ship and was boarded by Athenians.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Thrasybulus was the Athenian admiral with chief command on the day of the battle. He commanded the right wing with Pericles the younger and was later among the commanders involved in the controversy over the unburied dead.

l: Pericles the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Pericles the younger commanded the Athenian right wing with Thrasybulus. His ship engaged Callicratides’s vessel, which became fixed to it, allowing the Athenians to board and kill those aboard.

l: Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Theramenes commanded part of the Athenian right wing, having previously been a common soldier. He and Thrasybulus came to Athens before the other officers and sent letters blaming themselves for the failure to bury the dead; after he cleared himself, the people turned their anger against the other commanders.

l: Diomedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Diomedon was one of the condemned commanders and was described as an excellent soldier and a just man. Before his execution, he urged the Athenians to offer thanks to Jove, Apollo, and the glorious goddesses for the victory.

l: Sophocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Sophocles the tragedian, son of Theophilus, died at about ninety years of age. He had won eighteen victories upon the stage.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Athens incorporated many strangers and foreigners when the Athenians were weakened by continual losses. Its people later condemned the victorious commanders to death, then repented of the decision after the city came under thirty ruling masters.

l: Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenians sailed to Samos, where they joined other commanders who had assembled eighty additional galleys from other islands. They obtained ten more ships from the Samians before sailing to Arginusae.

l: Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Arginusae consisted of islands lying between Mitylene and Cuma near the continent and the promontory Catanides. The islands were inhabited and contained a small town peopled by the Eolians, and the Athenian fleet returned there after the storm.

l: Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: Mitylene was under siege when the Athenians sailed to Arginusae to relieve it. After the battle and storm, the Athenians reached Mitylene, took Conon and forty ships, and then went to Samos.

l: Athenian commanders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenian commanders arranged their fleet for battle and helped secure the victory at Arginusae. Eleven of them were later condemned to death and had their estates confiscated because the dead were not buried, although the storm had prevented that duty.

l: Athenian assembly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenian assembly initially applauded the commanders for the victory but became angry over the failure to bury the dead. It allowed the accusations to prevail, prevented the accused from being heard amid a tumult, and condemned the commanders to death.

l: Arginusae commanders’ trial and execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The commanders were ordered to return to Athens and were tried after the people heard accusations supported by the relatives of the dead. Eleven commanders were condemned to death, and they were led to execution despite having won the greatest sea-fight described as fought by Grecians against Grecians.

l: failure to bury the dead, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The dead could not be recovered because a violent storm shattered the ships and prevented the Athenians from reaching Mitylene or carrying out the burial. The failure nevertheless led to the commanders’ prosecution and execution at Athens.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenian fleet consisted of 150 ships assembled from sixty ships raised by the Athenians, eighty brought from other islands, and ten obtained from the Samians. It won at Arginusae but lost twenty-five ships and most of the men aboard them.

l: Spartan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Spartan fleet, commanded by Callicratides, consisted of 140 ships. It suffered a major defeat at Arginusae, losing seventy-seven ships, after which its surviving forces fled.

l: siege of Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The siege of Mitylene was being maintained by Etonicus while Callicratides sailed to meet the Athenians. After learning of the defeat, Etonicus withdrew his ships to Chios and marched his land army away to a neighboring city.

l: storm at Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: A violent storm arose after the battle and greatly damaged the ships. It prevented the Athenians from recovering the dead or sailing directly to Mitylene, forcing them back to Arginusae.

l: victory at Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIV.
s: The Athenians achieved a decisive victory at Arginusae after Callicratides was killed and the Lacedaemonian fleet fled. The victory was later overshadowed by the execution of the Athenian commanders for the failure to bury the dead.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Lysander assembled and supplied the Lacedaemonian fleet, captured Lampsacus, and defeated the Athenian fleet at Aegos Potamos. Conon escaped to Evagoras, while Philocles was captured and executed at Lampsacus. The Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians then blockaded Athens by land and sea, forcing the Athenians to surrender and accept the demolition of their fortifications, a ten-ship limit, and subjection to the Lacedaemonians. Thus the Peloponnesian War ended after twenty-seven years.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Athens was blockaded by land and sea after the destruction of the Athenian fleet. Driven by famine and other hardships, it surrendered and agreed to demolish its walls and the long fortifications of the Piraeus, keep no more than ten long ships, leave its other cities, and become subject to the Lacedaemonians.

l: Philocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Philocles was made general of the Athenian army and commanded the fleet jointly with Conon. At Aegos Potamos, he led thirty ships out of the harbour, was put to flight by Lysander, and was later captured and executed at Lampsacus.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Conon commanded the Athenian fleet jointly with Philocles. He escaped the defeat at Aegos Potamos with a few other commanders and, fearing to return to Athens, fled to Evagoras, prince of Cyprus.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The Athenian fleet numbered 173 ships at Samos, with twenty left there, and later assembled 180 ships for the Hellespont. Lysander surprised and captured it at Aegos Potamos, where only about ten of its commanders and officers escaped.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Lysander became high admiral of the Lacedaemonian fleet, raised ships, secured money and authority from Cyrus, and fitted out his forces at Ephesus. He captured Lampsacus, defeated and captured the Athenian fleet at Aegos Potamos, took Sestos, and then blockaded Samos and Athens.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The Lacedaemonians supported the oligarchic faction at Miletus and fought against Athens under Lysander. Their forces invaded Attica, blockaded Athens, and compelled the Athenians to accept subjection to them at the end of the war.

l: Peloponnesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The Peloponnesians refused to engage the Athenian fleet at first, allowing the Athenians to grow short of provisions. Under Lysander, they defeated the Athenian fleet, captured Sestos, and helped blockade Athens until its surrender.

l: Lampsacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Lampsacus was besieged and captured by Lysander. He dismissed its Athenian garrison, plundered the city, and restored it to its inhabitants; Philocles was later executed there.

l: Aegos Potamos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: Aegos Potamos was the place where the Athenian fleet anchored after the Athenians learned that Lampsacus had fallen. Lysander later surprised the fleet there and captured nearly all of its ships.

l: Piraeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The long fortifications of the Piraeus were required to be demolished as one of the terms imposed upon Athens at its surrender.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The Athenians challenged the Peloponnesians to battle at Aegos Potamos but were defeated when Lysander attacked while many of their men were ashore. Afterward they repaired and defended Athens, but famine forced them to surrender and accept severe conditions.

l: Aegeospotami naval battle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: At the Aegeospotami naval battle, Lysander exploited the disorder of the Athenian fleet and captured its ships after a brief resistance. Conon and a few other commanders escaped, while Philocles was taken prisoner and executed.

l: capture of Lampsacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The capture of Lampsacus was carried out by Lysander after he assembled a large navy. He dismissed the Athenian garrison, plundered the city, and restored it to its inhabitants.

l: siege of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The siege of Athens followed the defeat of the Athenian fleet. Agis and Pausanias invaded Attica while Lysander entered the Piraeus with more than two hundred ships, and the blockade caused severe famine in the city.

l: surrender of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The surrender of Athens occurred after famine caused many deaths in the city. Athens agreed to demolish its walls and the long fortifications of the Piraeus, keep no more than ten long ships, leave the other cities, and become subject to the Lacedaemonians.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XV.
s: The Peloponnesian War ended after the defeat of the Athenian fleet, the blockade of Athens, and the city's surrender. The text states that the war lasted twenty-seven years, making it the longest war known to the author.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Amilcar the Carthaginian sacked Agrigentum, devastated the country around Gela and Camarina, and besieged Gela. Dionysius brought an army to relieve Gela, but his forces were defeated and he withdrew, later ordering the inhabitants of Camarina to remove to Syracuse. The resulting anger led the Italians to leave his camp and the Syracusans to revolt, though Dionysius quickly returned to Syracuse and suppressed the rebellion. Amilcar then made peace with Dionysius, leaving several Sicilian cities under Carthaginian power or tribute, and the first Carthaginian war against Dionysius ended.

l: Amilcar the Carthaginian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Amilcar sacked Agrigentum, carried away valuable temple furnishings, devastated the territories of Gela and Camarina, and marched against Gela. After Dionysius withdrew and unrest broke out in Syracuse, Amilcar sent a herald to offer peace and concluded an agreement with Dionysius.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Dionysius gathered forces from Syracuse, Italy, and his confederates to relieve Gela, but his attack on the Carthaginian camp failed and he withdrew during the night. He ordered the inhabitants of Camarina to remove to Syracuse, provoking anger among his soldiers and subjects. He then hastened back to Syracuse, forced entry through the gates, killed or banished opponents, and made peace with Amilcar.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The Carthaginians sacked Agrigentum, devastated the country around Gela and Camarina, and besieged Gela with a fortified camp. They repelled Dionysius's attack before Gela, later entered Gela and plundered what had been left behind, and made peace after suffering heavy losses from plague.

l: Gelians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The Gelians resisted the siege by defending their walls, repairing breaches at night, and attacking Carthaginian stragglers. They briefly sallied to aid the Italians during the battle before Gela but returned to protect their walls. Afterward, they became incensed against Dionysius and turned off to Leontium.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The Syracusans helped Dionysius's forces, but many became hostile to him after the withdrawal from Gela and the forced removal of the people of Camarina. Syracusan horsemen rode to Syracuse, entered the arsenal, plundered Dionysius's palace, and abused his wife before Dionysius returned and crushed the revolt.

l: Grecians in Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The Italians attacked the Carthaginian camp near the shore during the battle before Gela. They were overpowered, lost more than a thousand men, and retreated into Gela. Afterward, all the Italians left Dionysius's camp and marched homeward.

l: Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Gela was besieged by Amilcar after the surrounding country was devastated. Its inhabitants resisted without effective aid from their confederates, but after Dionysius's failed relief attempt and nighttime withdrawal, the Carthaginians entered the city and plundered it.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Agrigentum was sacked by Amilcar at the return of spring. The Carthaginians carried away carved work and valuable furnishings from temples that had not been destroyed by fire.

l: Camarina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Camarina was devastated by Amilcar's forces. Dionysius later ordered its citizens, including their wives and children, to remove to Syracuse, and the people of Camarina subsequently became hostile to him and turned toward Leontium.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Syracuse received the inhabitants removed from Camarina and became the scene of a revolt against Dionysius. Syracusan horsemen entered the arsenal and plundered Dionysius's palace, but Dionysius returned, forced entry through the gates, and reestablished his control.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: Sicily was heavily affected by the war between the Carthaginians and Dionysius. The Carthaginians gained power over several Sicilian cities, while Leontium, Messania, and the other Sicilians were declared free under the peace terms, and Syracuse remained subject to Dionysius.

l: the first Carthaginian war against Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The first Carthaginian war against Dionysius ended after Amilcar's campaign against Gela, Dionysius's failed relief effort, and the unrest that followed his withdrawal. Peace was made with several cities placed under Carthaginian power or tribute and Syracuse left subject to Dionysius.

l: the siege of Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: During the siege of Gela, the Gelians defended their damaged walls, sent out troops against Carthaginian stragglers, and worked through the night to repair breaches. Dionysius eventually came with a large army, but the relief attack failed and he withdrew, after which the Carthaginians entered and plundered the city.

l: the battle before Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: In the battle before Gela, the Italians attacked the Carthaginian camp near the shore, while the Sicilians attacked elsewhere and Dionysius's mercenaries attempted to reach the Carthaginian engines. The Italians were driven back with heavy losses, the Sicilians also retreated after losing six hundred men, and Dionysius withdrew into Gela before abandoning the city.

l: the peace between Carthage and Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XVI.
s: The peace between Carthage and Dionysius gave the Carthaginians power over the Sicanians, Selinuntines, Agrigentines, and Himeraeans. Gela and Camarina could remain inhabited without walls but had to pay tribute, while Leontium, Messania, and the other Sicilians retained their laws and liberties; the Syracusans remained subject to Dionysius.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: After the Peloponnesian War, Athens obtained peace with the Lacedaemonians on condition that it demolish its walls and govern according to its own laws. Under pressure from Lysander, the Athenians abolished their democracy and appointed the Thirty, who established an oligarchic tyranny, executed Theramenes, confiscated property, and drove many citizens into exile. The Lacedaemonians supported the Thirty and ordered other Greek cities to return Athenian fugitives. In Sicily, Dionysius fortified Syracuse, but the Syracusans revolted and besieged him until Campanian forces enabled him to defeat and disperse them.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Athens was left in anarchy after its former government was dissolved. It obtained peace with the Lacedaemonians, demolished its walls, and then came under the rule of the Thirty.

l: the Thirty Tyrants of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Thirty Tyrants were appointed to govern Athens after Lysander pressured the Athenians to abolish the democracy. They filled offices with their supporters, summoned a Lacedaemonian garrison, executed wealthy citizens and other prominent men, and confiscated their property.

l: Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Theramenes opposed the establishment of the Thirty and argued that it violated the peace terms requiring Athens to be governed by its own laws. Although he was chosen as one of the Thirty because of his reputation for justice and moderation, he later resisted their abuses and was condemned and executed.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Lacedaemonians made peace with Athens and allowed it to govern according to its own laws if it demolished its walls. They later supplied a garrison to the Thirty and decreed that fugitives from Athens should be returned to them.

l: the Athenian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Athenian democracy was abolished by a general vote after Lysander threatened Theramenes and pressured the Athenians. Its replacement was the government of the Thirty.

l: the oligarchy of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The supporters of oligarchy in Athens appealed to Lysander to restore an earlier form of government. The oligarchy was established through the appointment of the Thirty, who ruled with the support of Lacedaemonian power.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Lysander advised the Athenians to choose thirty governors and threatened Theramenes when he opposed the proposal. He helped impose the oligarchic government after the peace with Athens.

l: the peace between Athens and Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The peace required Athens to demolish its walls and govern according to the laws of its own country. Lysander claimed that the Athenians had broken the agreement by failing to pull down their walls within the stipulated time.

l: the Thirty's government of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Thirty were charged with choosing the senate, creating magistrates, and making laws, but they delayed making laws while placing their supporters in offices. They brought in a foreign garrison, killed opponents and wealthy citizens, seized estates, and caused many inhabitants to flee.

l: Critias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Critias, the president of the Thirty, accused Theramenes before the senate of betraying the government. When Theramenes cleared himself and gained the senate's approval, Critias ordered soldiers to seize him.

l: the Thirty's execution of Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Thirty had Theramenes dragged from the senate-house altar by the lictors and led through the marketplace to execution. The people lamented his fate but did not rescue him because armed soldiers surrounded him.

l: the Thirty Years' tyranny in Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The tyranny of the Thirty grew increasingly violent after its rulers secured a Lacedaemonian garrison. They executed prominent and wealthy citizens, confiscated their estates, and reduced Athens so severely that more than half of its inhabitants fled.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, strengthened his control by fortifying the island and arsenal of Syracuse, distributing land and houses, and campaigning against free Sicilian communities. When the Syracusans revolted and besieged him, he sought aid from the Campanians, defeated the divided rebels, and then rewarded and dismissed the Campanians.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Dionysius divided the fortified island of Syracuse from the city, built towers and guardhouses, and enclosed the arsenal at the small harbor of Laccius. The city later became the center of a revolt against his rule.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Syracusans serving in Dionysius's army conspired to recover their liberty and killed the officer Doricus after he threatened a soldier. They besieged Dionysius, but divisions among them allowed him to attack and disperse them; more than seven thousand later surrendered.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: Dionysius sought to strengthen his rule in Sicily after making peace with the Carthaginians. He marched against Sicilian communities that remained free, especially those that had recently assisted the Carthaginians.

l: the revolt of the Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The revolt began when Syracusan soldiers killed Doricus and called for liberty. The rebels joined with horsemen from Enna, sought naval aid from Messana and Rhegium, and offered rewards and freedom to those who would help kill the tyrant.

l: the Syracusan siege of Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK XIV.
s: The Syracusans and their allies camped at the Epipolae, blocked Dionysius's passage, and attacked the island daily with siege engines. The siege weakened when Dionysius obtained Campanian aid, after which he sallied out and defeated the divided Syracusans.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: After the Peloponnesian War, the Lacedaemonians imposed oligarchies and tribute on many Greek cities and restored Lysander as high admiral. Dionysius strengthened his tyranny at Syracuse, while Alcibiades was killed after Pharnabazus revealed his plans to Artaxerxes. Clearchus established a brutal tyranny in Byzantium, was defeated by the Lacedaemonians at Porus, and later became a general for Cyrus. The Thebans subdued the Oropians, the Lacedaemonians invaded the Elei under Pausanias, and Dionysius planned war against Carthage while fortifying Epipolae.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: After the Lacedaemonians gained supremacy by sea and land, they appointed Lysander high admiral with authority to establish oligarchies in the cities. He later became prominent at Sparta and attempted to abolish the rule of the Heraclidae by promoting the idea that any Spartan should be eligible for kingship. He tried to bribe the oracles at Delphi, Dodona, and Jupiter Ammon, but failed; after his death, a speech advocating this change was found among his papers.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: After the Peloponnesian War, the Lacedaemonians held sovereign command by sea and land, imposed oligarchies and tribute on subdued cities, and sent governors to support their authority. They opposed Clearchus in Byzantium, defeated him at Porus, and later declared war against the Elei.

l: oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Lacedaemonians ordered an oligarchy to be established in every city because democrats were hostile to them. Some cities were governed by a decemvirate and others by an oligarchy.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Peloponnesian War had ended, leaving the Lacedaemonians with sovereign command by sea and land and enabling them to organize governments in the Greek cities.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Dionysius strengthened his tyranny at Syracuse by disarming the citizens, building another wall around the castle, hiring foreign troops, and preparing whatever was necessary to secure his rule. He conquered or subjugated Enna, Catana, Naxos, and Leontium, and later planned war against Carthage while fortifying Epipolae.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Syracuse was placed under stronger tyrannical control when Dionysius seized weapons from the citizens and recruited foreign troops. Its inhabitants of Naxos, Catana, and Leontium were defeated, enslaved, expelled, or transferred under Dionysius's expansion.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Alcibiades learned that Cyrus was secretly preparing war against Artaxerxes and sought help from Pharnabazus to reach the Persian king. When Pharnabazus refused, Alcibiades traveled toward Paphlagonia, but enemies surrounded his lodging in Phrygia, burned it, and killed him with fire and missiles.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Pharnabazus learned of Alcibiades's intended disclosure to Artaxerxes and sent a messenger to reveal the conspiracy first. He later refused Alcibiades a passport and arranged for men to ambush and kill him.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Cyrus secretly prepared with the Lacedaemonians to make war against his brother Artaxerxes. After Clearchus fled to Ionia, Cyrus became familiar with him, gave him money, and ordered him to raise an army of foreign soldiers.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Artaxerxes was the Persian king and the brother whom Cyrus intended to attack. Alcibiades planned to inform him of Cyrus's conspiracy, but Pharnabazus disclosed it first.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Byzantium suffered from internal seditions and wars with neighboring Thracians and requested a governor from the Lacedaemonians. Clearchus took control, murdered magistrates and prominent citizens, confiscated property, and ruled as a tyrant until the Lacedaemonians attacked him.

l: Clearchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Clearchus was sent to govern Byzantium but gathered mercenaries and acted as a tyrant, killing magistrates and leading citizens, confiscating their goods, and banishing others. Defeated by the Lacedaemonians at Porus, he escaped to Selymbria and later to Ionia, where Cyrus made him a general.

l: the Heraclidae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Heraclidae held the royal power at Sparta. Lysander planned to end their rule by arranging that any Spartan could be chosen king.

l: the Spartan kingship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Lysander sought to change the Spartan kingship so that the king could be chosen from any Spartan family rather than only from the families of the Heraclidae. He attempted to secure support for this plan by bribing several oracles, without success.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Thebans assisted exiles from Oropus after the Oropians had expelled them. They seized Oropus, moved its inhabitants farther from the sea, and eventually brought them under the same government as themselves, joining their lands to Boeotia.

l: the Elei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Elei refused the Lacedaemonians' demands that neighboring cities govern themselves and contribute to the costs of the war against the Athenians. They defended their city with help from citizens and Etolian soldiers, killed about thirty of Pausanias's men in a sortie, and endured the destruction of their countryside.

l: Pausanias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Pausanias led a Lacedaemonian army against the Elei, captured Lasion, Threstus, Aulis, Eupagium, Opus, and Pylos, and camped near Elis. He failed to take the city, ravaged the surrounding country, fortified castles, and wintered in Dyme.

l: Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Epipolae overlooked Syracuse and was considered capable of commanding the city. Dionysius therefore selected it as the site for a major defensive fortification.

l: the Epipolae fortification, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Dionysius ordered a fortification at Epipolae with six gates, towers, and a wall thirty furlongs long. Sixty thousand freemen and six thousand yoke of oxen were employed, and the wall was completed in twenty days.

l: the war between Dionysius and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: After making peace with the Carthaginians, Dionysius decided to make war against them. He kept the plan secret while preparing, and strengthened Syracuse first by fortifying Epipolae.

l: the war against the Elei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Lacedaemonians used complaints about the Elei's treatment of Pausanias and their exclusion of Spartans from the Olympic games as pretexts for war. Pausanias invaded Elis, captured several places, but failed to conquer the city and spent the winter in Dyme.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus, supported by the Lacedaemonians and Greek mercenaries, raised an army and marched from Asia through Cilicia and Syria toward Babylon to challenge his brother, Artaxerxes, for the Persian kingdom. Artaxerxes assembled a much larger army and met Cyrus near the Euphrates, where the Grecians routed the forces opposing them. Cyrus wounded Artaxerxes with a javelin but was then mortally wounded and killed by a Persian soldier, causing his army to lose the battle. The Greek forces nevertheless defeated the barbarians who attacked them after Cyrus's death.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus secretly prepared an expedition against his brother Artaxerxes, gathering about seventy thousand men from Asia and thirteen thousand Greek mercenaries. He marched through Cilicia and across the Euphrates toward Babylon, disclosed his design to the army only gradually, and promised rewards to secure its continued support. In the battle, he struck Artaxerxes down with a javelin but was mortally wounded by a common Persian soldier and died.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Artaxerxes learned of Cyrus's preparations and assembled forces from throughout his territories. He marched against Cyrus with an army that Ephorus estimated at no fewer than four hundred thousand horse and foot. Cyrus wounded him in battle, but he was carried from the fight as if dead; his troops later recovered and defeated Cyrus's army.

l: war between Cyrus and Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The war arose from Cyrus's attempt to seize the Persian kingdom from his brother Artaxerxes. Cyrus marched through Asia and across the Euphrates, while Artaxerxes gathered a much larger army and met him near Babylon. Cyrus was killed in the battle, and Artaxerxes's forces ultimately prevailed.

l: Grecian forces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The Grecian forces included Lacedaemonians and other Greek mercenaries serving under Cyrus. They fought with greater skill than the lightly armed and inexperienced barbarians, routed the forces opposing them, and later repelled another attack after Cyrus's death.

l: march out of Persia into Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus's army made a long and difficult march from Asia toward Babylon, passing through Cilicia, Syria, and the narrow gates and mountain passes on the way. The soldiers feared the reported distance to Bactria and the many hostile nations along the route, but continued after Cyrus promised them increased pay and rewards.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The Lacedaemonians decided that Cyrus's war would benefit them and ordered aid to be sent to him. They directed their admiral Samus to obey Cyrus, sent a fleet, and dispatched eight hundred soldiers under Chirosophus while keeping their support officially secret.

l: Chirosophus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Chirosophus commanded the eight hundred Lacedaemonian soldiers sent to support Cyrus. He delivered the troops to Cyrus at Issus, where they were presented as having been sent privately by Cyrus's friends.

l: Cilicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus's army passed through the narrow and rugged gates leading into Cilicia and marched to Tarsus, which it forced to submit. Syennesis, king of Cilicia, promised Cyrus assistance while secretly informing Artaxerxes about the expedition.

l: Clearchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Clearchus commanded the Peloponnesians except the Achaians and led the Lacedaemonians and some mercenaries in the right wing. He ordered the Grecians to run in upon the enemy at close range, and later stopped his men from pursuing too far because he feared the barbarians would cut them off.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The Persians led the barbarian contingents in their respective companies and regiments. Their forces included many lightly armed or inexperienced soldiers, but a Persian common soldier mortally wounded Cyrus, and the royalist Persians recovered after his death and defeated his army.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus crossed the Euphrates with his army after gaining the soldiers' agreement to continue the expedition. Artaxerxes encamped by the river, left his heavy baggage behind a trench, and fought Cyrus's forces near its borders.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus promised every soldier a mina when he reached Babylon. After crossing the Euphrates, he marched toward Babylon and allowed the army to refresh itself when it reached the borders of the country.

l: Tissaphernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Tissaphernes, a noble Persian, took Artaxerxes's place when the king was carried from the battle as if dead. He encouraged the soldiers, fought valiantly, and killed many of Cyrus's men while attempting to avenge the king.

l: the battle of Cunaxa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The battle was fought between Cyrus's Greek-supported army and Artaxerxes's Persian forces near Babylon. The Grecians routed the forces opposing them, but Cyrus was killed after striking Artaxerxes, and the royalists eventually overcame Cyrus's main army. The Grecians then defeated the barbarians who attacked them after nightfall.

l: Cyrus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Cyrus's army consisted of about seventy thousand men from Asia, thirteen thousand Greek mercenaries, and additional forces gathered during the march. It crossed the Euphrates and fought Artaxerxes's much larger army, but lost its leader and was ultimately defeated, although the Greek contingent remained victorious in its own engagements.

l: Artaxerxes's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: Artaxerxes's army was assembled from many regions and was estimated by Ephorus at no fewer than four hundred thousand horse and foot. It initially suffered defeat against the Grecians, but after Cyrus was killed it recovered, plundered Cyrus's camp, and defeated his main forces.

l: Greek mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V-
s: The Greek mercenaries were drawn from the Peloponnesus and other parts of Greece and numbered about thirteen thousand. They were commanded in separate contingents by Clearchus, Proxenus, Socrates, and Menon, fought with skill gained from the Peloponnesian War, and repeatedly routed the less experienced barbarians.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: After Cyrus was killed and Artaxerxes's forces won the battle, Clearchus and the Greek army refused to surrender their arms and arranged a retreat toward the sea. Artaxerxes granted them a truce, but Tissaphernes later treacherously seized and killed their commanders, after which the Greeks elected Chirosophus as their general. The Greeks fought and suffered through the country of the Carduchi, Armenia, and other regions before reaching Trapezus and eventually Chrysopolis. The unit concludes with the hardships and progress of the Greek retreat, including the Armenian snowstorm and the honey poisoning.

l: Clearchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: After making a great slaughter among the king's forces, Clearchus erected a trophy and returned to camp. He refused Artaxerxes's demand that the Greeks surrender their arms, led the army toward the sea, and later went with the other commanders to Tissaphernes, who seized him and had him killed.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: After Cyrus's death, Aridaeus returned to his former post and asked Clearchus to join forces with him near the sea. He was included with the mercenaries whose peaceful passage was promised, but Tissaphernes later used him as part of the scheme to destroy the Greeks.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Artaxerxes defeated Cyrus's forces, demanded that the Greeks lay down their arms, and later granted them a three-day truce to pass through his country with guides and provisions. He returned to Babylon, rewarded Tissaphernes and other courageous soldiers, and had the captured Greek commanders put to death except Menon.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Cyrus was killed in the battle against Artaxerxes. His death caused fear throughout his army and led the Greeks to plan their retreat.

l: Tissaphernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Artaxerxes rewarded Tissaphernes for being judged the bravest man, gave him a marriage alliance, and appointed him governor and lieutenant of the provinces formerly commanded by Cyrus on the sea-coast. Tissaphernes persuaded Artaxerxes to let him pursue the Greeks, then treacherously summoned and seized Clearchus and the other commanders and attacked the retreating Greeks without facing their whole army.

l: Chirosophus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: After the Greek commanders were massacred, Chirosophus was chosen as general by the soldiers. He was sent to Byzantium to obtain ships, but returned after failing to secure them.

l: Grecian forces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Greeks refused to surrender their arms after Cyrus's defeat and negotiated a temporary truce with Artaxerxes. After their commanders were massacred, they elected new officers under Chirosophus, fought their way through several hostile countries, reached the sea at the mountain Chenius, and eventually arrived at Chrysopolis.

l: Artaxerxes's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Persian army defeated Cyrus's forces, killing more than fifteen thousand on the king's side and pursuing the Greeks after their retreat. Under Tissaphernes, it attacked stragglers and pursued the Greeks as far as the country of the Carduchi, but did not dare confront their entire army.

l: Greek mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The mercenaries under Clearchus and Aridaeus were included in the agreement allowing them to pass peacefully through the king's territory, provided they committed no outrages. They formed the principal body of the Greek army during the retreat.

l: the Carduchi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Carduchi were a free and warlike people hostile to the king and skilled with slings and powerful bows. They attacked the Greeks from the higher ground and inflicted many deaths and wounds.

l: Paphlagonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Paphlagonia was selected as the direction of the Greek march toward the sea. The Greeks later passed through areas associated with Paphlagonia and its neighboring regions.

l: Armenia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Greeks crossed the river Centrites into Armenia, which was governed by Teribazus for the king. They initially passed through the province under an agreement of friendship but then endured severe winter conditions in the Armenian mountains.

l: the country of the Carduchi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Greeks reached the country of the Carduchi after Tissaphernes pursued them. They suffered attacks from the inhabitants for seven days while crossing its mountains before reaching the river Centrites.

l: Trapezus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Trapezus was described as a Greek city and a colony of the Sinopians belonging to the Colchians. The Greeks stayed there for thirty days, received generous hospitality, sacrificed to Hercules and Jupiter Soter, celebrated gymnic games, and obtained two small vessels.

l: Chrysopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Chrysopolis, a city of Chalcedonia, was the place where the surviving Greeks eventually arrived after crossing Bithynia. Only three thousand eight hundred of the original ten thousand were said to remain when they reached it.

l: the battle of Cunaxa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: In the battle, Cyrus was killed and Artaxerxes's forces became victorious, while Clearchus's Lacedaemonians and mercenaries inflicted most of the king's casualties. More than fifteen thousand were killed on the king's side, about three thousand in Cyrus's army, and few Greeks were killed.

l: Cyrus's expedition against Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Cyrus's expedition against Artaxerxes ended with Cyrus's death and the defeat of his forces. The surviving Greeks then began their long retreat toward the sea and eventually returned toward their own country.

l: the Greek retreat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Greek retreat proceeded through the country of the Carduchi, Armenia, the lands of the Chaonians, Phasians, Chalcidonians, Tascutians, Macrones, Colchians, and others. The Greeks faced hostile inhabitants, difficult mountains, winter storms, shortages, and repeated attacks before reaching Greek cities and eventually Chrysopolis.

l: the commanders' massacre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: Tissaphernes summoned Clearchus and the other Greek commanders to his tent under the pretense of discussion. After a purple flag was raised, the commanders were seized, those outside were killed, and the captured commanders were sent in chains to Artaxerxes, who put them to death except Menon.

l: the crossing of the Carduchian mountains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: The Greeks spent seven days crossing the mountains of the Carduchi and suffered heavily from attacks by the inhabitants. The Carduchi used elevated positions, slings, and unusually large bows and arrows against them.

l: the Armenian snowstorm, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: While crossing the Armenian mountains, the Greeks encountered deep snow, freezing cold, hail, and violent wind. They were forced to remain where the storm found them, losing men, animals, and the use of some fingers and toes before reaching villages with underground shelters and supplies.

l: the honey poisoning, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Clearchus, after he had made a great slaughter among them, (it
s: In the country of the Colchians, many Greeks ate honeycombs and immediately became mad and lay on the ground as if dead. By the same hour the next day they recovered their senses and strength, and three days later the army reached Trapezus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Thrasybulus and the Athenian exiles overthrew the Thirty Tyrants, took the Piraeus, and helped restore Athens to its ancient laws, while opponents were allowed to withdraw to Eleusis. Sparta intervened through Pausanias, reconciling the exiles and citizens, while Lysander had been summoned by the new Athenian decemvirs. In Asia, Tissaphernes threatened the Greek cities, prompting Sparta to send Thimbron and later Dercyllidas against the Persian king; Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes meanwhile helped organize a Persian fleet under Conon. The unit also recounts Psammetichus's murder of Tamos, Xenophon's campaign against the Thracians, Socrates' trial and execution, and the fortification of the Chersonesus of Thrace.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Thrasybulus, surnamed Tyrius and an Athenian citizen, fled the Thirty Tyrants and, with Theban assistance, seized Phila. He defeated the tyrants' forces, took Munychia and the Piraeus, rejected their offer to share power, and helped restore the Athenian citizens to their former liberties.

l: the Thirty Tyrants of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Thirty Tyrants continued banishing and executing Athenians and used foreign soldiers to control Athens. They were defeated by Thrasybulus's forces, expelled from the city, and replaced by a decemvirate.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Athens was controlled by the Thirty Tyrants until the exiles and their supporters took the Piraeus and compelled political change. The Athenians were eventually restored to the city and governed according to their ancient laws.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Thebans were angered by the cruelty of the Thirty Tyrants and courteously received Athenian exiles. They secretly aided Thrasybulus in seizing Phila.

l: Phila, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Phila was a very strong castle about one hundred stages from Athens. Thrasybulus secretly seized it with assistance from Thebes, giving the exiles a position from which Attica could easily be invaded.

l: Piraeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Thrasybulus marched against the Piraeus after defeating the forces gathered at Acarnas and seized Munychia there. His forces later gained possession of the Piraeus, where many opponents of the tyranny and Athenian exiles joined him.

l: Critias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Critias commanded the Thirty Tyrants' attack on Munychia. He was killed during the sharp engagement, after which the tyrants' forces withdrew.

l: the Athenian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenian exiles gathered around Thrasybulus and grew numerous after his successes. They helped defeat the tyrants, seized the Piraeus, besieged Athens, and were eventually restored to their country.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Athenian citizens who had no share in the government with the three thousand became eager to dissolve the rule of the Thirty Tyrants. They were eventually reconciled with the exiles and restored to their country.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Sparta received requests for aid from the Thirty Tyrants but later intervened in Athens through Pausanias. It also sent Thimbron and Dercyllidas to oppose Persian power in Asia and imposed terms on Elis and Messenia.

l: Pausanias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Pausanias, then king of Lacedaemon, marched with a large army to Athens. Out of envy toward Lysander and concern about Greek hostility to Sparta, he reconciled the Athenian exiles and citizens.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenian decemvirs summoned Lysander from Lacedaemon with forty ships and a thousand soldiers. Pausanias opposed his influence by marching to Athens and arranging a reconciliation.

l: Messenia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Sparta prepared for war against Messenia after making peace with its neighbors. The Messenians were expelled from their settlements in Cephallenia and Naupactus and driven from Greece.

l: Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Messenians were expelled by the Lacedaemonians because of the ancient hatred between them. Some went to Sicily and served under Dionysius, while about three thousand went to Cyrene and joined its exiles, where nearly all were killed in battle.

l: Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Cyrene suffered a great civil conflict after Aristocrates and others seized the city and five hundred leading citizens were suddenly killed. Its exiles joined the Messenians in attacking the city, and the Cyrenians later ended their internal conflict by swearing to forget past injuries.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Artaxerxes, king of Asia, defeated Cyrus and sent Tissaphernes to take charge of the governments on the sea-coasts. His decision whether there would be peace or war was later awaited during the truce between Dercyllidas and Pharnabazus.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Cyrus was defeated by Artaxerxes. Some of the soldiers who had accompanied him against his brother returned to Greece, while others followed Xenophon.

l: Tissaphernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Tissaphernes was appointed by Artaxerxes to govern the sea-coast territories and threatened cities that had supported Cyrus. He attacked the Cumeans, ravaged their countryside, took prisoners, and later raised a large force with Pharnabazus against the Lacedaemonians.

l: Tamos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Tamos, the chief lord-lieutenant of Ionia, feared Tissaphernes and fled to Egypt with his wealth and children, except Gaus. Psammetichus murdered Tamos, his children, and his attendants to obtain their money and ships.

l: Psammetichus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Psammetichus, king of Egypt and a descendant of the ancient Psammetichus, had previously received benefits from Tamos. He nevertheless murdered Tamos, his children, and his attendants out of covetousness.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Egypt was ruled by Psammetichus, to whom Tamos fled for protection from Tissaphernes. Psammetichus violated the law of nations by murdering Tamos and those who sought refuge with him.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Persian Empire, represented by Artaxerxes, sought to reassert control over the governments and Greek cities on the sea-coasts after Cyrus's defeat. Persian forces under Tissaphernes and Pharnabazus opposed the Lacedaemonians.

l: the Greek cities of Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Greek cities of Asia feared destruction after Tissaphernes's arrival and sent ambassadors to Sparta for protection. They also sent messengers to Tissaphernes in an effort to secure his favor.

l: Thimbron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Thimbron was appointed by the Lacedaemonians to command the war against the Persian king with a thousand Spartans and authority to raise additional allied troops. He reached Ephesus with about seven thousand men, took Magnesia, failed to take Tralles, and withdrew to Ephesus when Tissaphernes approached.

l: the war against the Persian king, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The war against the Persian king began as a Lacedaemonian response to Persian attacks on the Greek cities of Asia. Thimbron first led the campaign, and Dercyllidas was later sent to replace him because the war was being badly managed.

l: Ephesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Ephesus served as Thimbron's base after he crossed from Corinth and later as his place of retreat when Tissaphernes approached. Dercyllidas also commanded an army there when the Persian forces advanced.

l: Xenophon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Xenophon was chosen general by nearly five thousand soldiers who had served with Cyrus. He led them against the Thracians of Salmydessus, burned many towns and villages, and then marched to join Thimbron after being promised pay.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Thracians near Salmydessus were known for seizing shipwrecked merchants who reached the shore and carrying them away as captives. Xenophon defeated them and burned many of their towns and villages; other Thracians later invaded the Chersonesus of Thrace.

l: Socrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Socrates was accused by Anytus and Melitus of atheism and corrupting the youth. He was condemned and executed by drinking poison, an act that the Athenians soon regretted.

l: Dercyllidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Dercyllidas was sent by the Lacedaemonians to replace Thimbron as general in Asia. He quickly captured cities in the territory of Troas, fought the Thracians in Bithynia, later expelled them from the Chersonesus of Thrace, and returned to Asia.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Pharnabazus agreed to an eight-month truce with Dercyllidas and later persuaded the Persian king to equip a fleet and appoint Conon as admiral. He raised forces with Tissaphernes and marched toward Ephesus, where a further truce was arranged.

l: the Chersonesus of Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Chersonesus of Thrace was invaded and ravaged by large bodies of Thracians, who seized its fortified cities. Dercyllidas drove them out and built a wall from one sea to the other, protecting the region from further incursions.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Conon, an Athenian soldier serving with Evagoras in Cyprus, was appointed admiral of the Persian fleet at Pharnabazus's recommendation. He accepted in hopes of recovering the sea's sovereignty for Athens and sailed with forty ships to Cilicia while the fleet was being completed.

l: the Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Persian fleet was planned and equipped after Pharnabazus persuaded the king to continue preparations for war. Conon was appointed its admiral, though he initially sailed with only forty ships to Cilicia because the full fleet was not ready.

l: Socrates' trial and execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Socrates' trial and execution followed accusations by Anytus and Melitus that he was an atheist and corrupted the youth. After Socrates was put to death by poison, the Athenians regretted the decision and killed his accusers without waiting for legal formalities.

l: the Athenian restoration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenian restoration followed Pausanias's intervention after the exiles had taken the Piraeus and the city had expelled the Thirty Tyrants. The exiles and citizens were reconciled, Athens resumed government according to its ancient laws, and those fearing punishment could withdraw to Eleusis.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius made peace with the Rhegians and Messanians, then prepared a large-scale war against the Carthaginians by building ships, weapons, armor, artillery engines, and military facilities. He secured support from many Sicilian cities, married Doris of Locris and Aristomache of Syracuse, and persuaded the Syracusans to approve war against Carthage. Dionysius declared that the Carthaginians should restore the Greek cities they had subdued and then marched against Motya, while most Sicilian cities submitted to him. The Carthaginians, weakened by a plague, sent a night raid that destroyed most of the ships in Syracuse's harbor, while Dionysius continued the siege of Motya.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius made peace with the Rhegians and Messanians before undertaking extensive preparations for war against Carthage. He assembled a large army and fleet, gained the submission or support of most Sicilian cities, declared war against the Carthaginians, and besieged Motya.

l: Rhegians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Rhegians feared Dionysius's growing power because he had enslaved the Naxians and Cataneans, who were related to them. They attempted to make war against him with Syracusan exiles, but withdrew when the Messanian troops mutinied, and later made peace with Dionysius.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Carthaginians were weakened by a severe plague and were unprepared when Dionysius declared war. They sent an admiral with ten galleys to raid Syracuse at night, and their forces later prepared to raise troops in Europe.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Syracusans assisted Dionysius in producing ships, weapons, and military equipment. They approved his proposal for war against the Carthaginians, seized Carthaginian property in Syracuse, and supplied citizens as masters, pilots, and rowers for half of the long ships.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Syracuse became the center of Dionysius's extensive military preparations, with workmen producing arms, ships, and artillery engines throughout the city. Its harbor was attacked at night by a Carthaginian force, which destroyed or sank almost all the ships there.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Carthage was presented with Dionysius's demand that it restore the Greek cities it had subdued to their ancient laws and liberties. Its senate and people were alarmed by the declaration of war because the plague had destroyed many people and the city lacked necessary preparations.

l: Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Motya was a strong Carthaginian colony situated on an island near Sicily and served as an important castle and inlet. It resisted Dionysius while expecting aid from Carthage, and Dionysius returned with his army to besiege it.

l: war between the Rhegians and Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Rhegians initiated preparations for war against Dionysius because they feared suffering the same fate as the Naxians and Cataneans. The campaign ended without a battle after the Messanian soldiers rejected their commanders and returned home, prompting the Rhegians to withdraw and later seek peace.

l: war between Carthage and Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius prepared for war against Carthage by raising troops, constructing ships and weapons, and seeking support from Sicilian cities and foreign soldiers. He declared war unless Carthage restored the Greek cities under its control, then marched toward Eryx and Motya.

l: siege of Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius besieged Motya after most of the surrounding Sicilian cities had submitted to him. He filled the channel between the island and the shore with stone and rubble so that his forces could bring their artillery engines closer to the town.

l: the plague in the Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: A plague raged in Africa and swept away many Carthaginians. Dionysius treated the plague as an opportunity to attack while Carthage was weakened, and the Carthaginians were consequently unprepared for war.

l: Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Rhegium supported the Syracusan exiles when they attempted to campaign against Dionysius. Later, its council rejected Dionysius's proposal that it provide him with a woman of the city as a wife, despite his offer of land and assistance.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Many cities in Sicily joined Dionysius as he marched toward Motya because they hated Carthaginian rule and hoped to recover their liberties. Most of the cities submitted to him, while Ancyra, Segesta, Panormus, and Egesta remained opposed.

l: Syracusan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius built more than two hundred galleys, refitted one hundred and ten, and repaired or covered one hundred and fifty older vessels. A Carthaginian night raid in the harbor of Syracuse destroyed almost all the ships stationed there.

l: siege engines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The art of making engines for hurling large stones was first practiced at Syracuse during Dionysius's preparations. He ordered artillery engines of many designs, and later used them in the approaches against Motya.

l: arms and armor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius ordered large quantities of weapons and armor, including one hundred and forty thousand shields, swords, and helmets, and fourteen thousand corslets. He intended soldiers from different countries to use the offensive and defensive arms customary in their own nations.

l: Carthaginian night raid on Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Himilco secretly sent an admiral with ten galleys to Syracuse, intending to destroy the ships in the harbor and force Dionysius to divide his forces. Entering at night, the admiral broke up, sank, and destroyed almost all the ships he found there before returning toward Carthage.

l: Dionysius's military preparation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius gathered craftsmen from his dominions, Italy, and Greece, organized the production of weapons and ships, constructed harbor facilities, and recruited soldiers from Sicily, Greece, and especially Lacedaemon. He ultimately assembled an army of about eighty thousand foot soldiers and more than three thousand horsemen for the campaign.

l: Dionysius's speech for war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius told the Syracusans that the Carthaginians were implacable enemies of the Grecians and were continually plotting to ruin the Sicilians. He argued that they should be attacked while weakened by the plague rather than after they had recovered their strength.

l: Carthaginian enslavement of Greek cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Dionysius accused the Carthaginians of having subdued Greek cities and depriving them of their laws and liberties. He used this grievance to demand their restoration and to persuade the Syracusans and other Greeks to support the war.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, About this very time, Himiico, the Carthaginian general^ hearing
s: Himiico sailed from Carthage with one hundred galleys and attacked Dionysius's ships at Motya, destroying some and burning others, but he withdrew when he could not defeat the larger Syracusan force. Dionysius completed a rampart and used battering engines and tall siege towers to breach Motya's walls. After a prolonged assault, his army entered the city by night and overcame the Motyans. The Sicilians massacred many inhabitants and plundered the city, while Dionysius sold surviving citizens into slavery, except for certain prisoners whom he ordered to be executed.

s: Himiico, the Carthaginian general, sailed from Carthage with one hundred galleys to make a surprise attack on Dionysius's fleet at Motya. He destroyed some ships and burned others, but withdrew to Africa after failing to overcome the enemy's defenses and larger force.

s: Dionysius prevented Himiico from bringing his ships out through Motya's narrow harbor and had them drawn overland into the sea at a safer distance. He then completed the siege works, captured Motya, ordered the surviving citizens to seek refuge in the Greek temples, and returned to Syracuse after placing a garrison in the city.
